newsitem.title: UK: Sterling keeps pressure on mark in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sterling keeps pressure on mark in late Europe.

text.p: Sterling ended European trading more than two pfennigs higher on the day, drawing strength from a buoyant dollar and rosier than expected UK public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) data, traders and analysts said.
"It's on the back of dollar/mark and the better than expected PSBR numbers -- the market's thin as well," said a senior dealer at a UK bank in London.
Data showed a 36 million sterling public sector debt surplus, confounding forecasts of a 1.7 billion deficit.
"The economy is growing above trend and that's resulting in much better budget deficit figures than the market has been prepared for," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB here.
The UK Treasury warned, however, that the number should be viewed with caution as it had been flattered by asset sales and changes to big companies' tax payments.

The pound was quoted at 2.7978/88 marks at 1427 GMT versus 2.7728/33 in late Europe on Friday. Cable drifted at $1.6396/06 versus late Friday's $1.6377/82 but its stability gave sterling/mark a springboard, dealers said.
"Cable has support around the $1.6350 level so while it holds above there, with a bid dollar environment there's always a tendency for the cross to move high," said one.
With the market awaiting new UK Chancellor Gordon Brown's mini-budget, analysts said the public borrowing data would diminish the case for aggressive tax hikes.
"The argument for tax increases to shore up the public finances is actually not that well-founded," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel here.

"My view is taxes should still increase, but with the specific objective of hitting consumer spending rather than to fill any black hole in public finances, because I'm not convinced there is one," he added.
That implies interest rates should rise further, and is therefore supportive for sterling, Cole said.

The UK base interest rate was increased by a quarter-point on May 6, but many have been arguing that the ongoing strength of sterling and consumer demand mean fiscal rather than monetary policy should now be tightened.
